turns.t: Mr Doherty? I'm Fidelma, I'll take your temperature and pulse first. Sit there. ~
Thank you. I have a painful right ear, and I can barely hear out of it. Since Sunday.
Temperature 37.0, pulse 72.
Good morning, Mr Doherty. How did the ear start?
I swam in the sea on Saturday, and the water got in, and by Sunday it was blocked, then painful.
How would you describe the pain?
A throbbing ache, severe when I touch the ear, or pull on it, or chew. It wakes me at night.
Any discharge?
A little clear fluid, yesterday. Today it's gone.
Any dizziness, or ringing?
No. Neither.
Any allergies to medicines?
Ciprofloxacin gave me a rash, years ago, so I avoid that.
That's useful. Any health conditions, like diabetes?
No, nothing. I'm fit as a flea.
Do you swim regularly, or use earbuds?
I swim in the sea three times a week, and I use earphones to run.
Let me look in your ear. This may be uncomfortable.
Ow. Ow. ~
The ear canal is swollen and red, with some debris, and pulling the ear is very painful. I can't see the eardrum properly.
Doctor, he flinched a lot. ~
It's an infection of the ear canal, outer ear, we call it otitis externa, swimmer's ear.
Can you treat it? ~
Yes. I'm going to prescribe ear drops with an antibiotic and a steroid, three drops, three times a day, for seven days.
In the right ear? ~
Yes. Lie on your side, put the drops in, and stay there for five minutes. ~
Okay. ~
And I'd like you to take paracetamol for the pain, 1 gram, up to four times a day.
Right. ~
Keep the ear dry, no swimming, no earphones, and don't poke anything in it.
How long off swimming? ~
Until it's completely better, at least two weeks. ~
I'll clean the ear gently, if you like, doctor, before he uses the drops. ~
Please do, Fidelma. And if the swelling closes the canal, the nurse may put in a small wick. ~
Okay. ~
If the pain gets worse, you get a fever, swelling behind the ear, or dizziness, come back the same day.
I will. Thank you. ~
